newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: FOCUS - Slow start to mining in Central Asia.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Slow start to mining in Central Asia.

text.p: A base metals deposit high up in the scrub-covered mountains of Uzbekistan's Khandiza Valley is the center of rare mining activity in far-flung Central Asia.

"We're pioneers here," said Richard Wilkins, commercial director of Oxus Resources Corp, as he splashed in khaki shorts and rubber boots through puddles in an inky mine shaft dug by the Soviets at the company's Khandiza base metal deposit.
At the shaft entrance, Uzbek and British geologists poured over rock samples above a river gushing through a scorched brown gulley, marked with stunted hawthorne trees.
"We'll be the first foreign company to mine base metals in Uzbekistan," said Wilkins.

He said Khandiza, located in the southeast of the former Soviet republic, would require $104 million in capital and would produce about 85,000 tonnes per year (tpy) of zinc, 36,000 tpy of lead and 11,000 tpy of copper.
"It will take about three to four years to bring Khandiza into production," Wilkins said.

That a foreign company should only now be looking at producing base metals in Central Asia, nearly six years after the ex-Soviet states found themselves independent of Moscow, underlines the snail-paced development of the region's potentially rich mining sector.

Wilkins said Central Asia got itself a bad name in the early days after independence when large and small companies piled in expecting a new Klondike, only to find themselves caught in complex legal tangles, corruption and general post-Soviet chaos.
"Now most of the republics have new legal codes, they promise investor protection," said Wilkins. "In the early days, I used to come with suitcases of cash -- now I can get it wired to a bank."
Despite the changes -- mobile telephones operate even inside the capital of war-ravaged Tajikistan -- the region's mining sector attracts only a fraction of the big money going into oil and gas.

British conglomerate Lonrho Plc actually pulled out of the $350 million Amantaitau gold project in Uzbekistan this month, unable, say Uzbek mining officials, to find a partner to share development costs.

Uzbek officials said Canada's Cameco and Teck Corp were now negotiating to develop Amantaitau, which could produce 10 to 14 tonnes of gold annually over 12 to 17 years. But the republic is a notoriously slow partner to deal with, and the state insists on a major shareholding in all projects.
"There's still a very Soviet mentality here," said a senior Uzbek mining official on condition of anonymity. "This has got to change," he said.

Anxious to bring investment to impoverished places like Khandiza, where the birth rate has fallen three times since 1990, mining companies say Central Asian governments have worked to make mining projects more attractive.
But outside factors now cloud prospects for mining the region's mountains, deserts and steppe.

The aftershocks from Indonesia's Bre-X scandal, in which a much hyped gold deposit was found eventually to be worthless, are felt throughout Central Asia by mining companies like Oxus looking for cash.
Oxus is hoping to raise $12 million in development capital in a planned November listing on the Toronto stock exchange.
"I can understand why the market's nervous after Bre-X," said Wilkins, "but there's no comparison to the thorough data we have from the Soviet era. This is no scam."

Mining companies in the region have also been hit by low metals prices, especially gold which is languishing at 12-year lows. The price has seen Oxus mothball one of its own gold projects in Kazakhstan.
